newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Marchelli says EMU needs political body.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Marchelli says EMU needs political body.

text.p: Europe needs a strong political body to oversee monetary union to ensure the region is run as a democracy rather than a technocracy, a member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council said on Wednesday.
In an interview with Reuters, Paul Marchelli said an EU summit in Dublin this weekend would be a landmark which could define future decisions about policies towards Europe.
"After Dublin, we will have to take stock to see if the results allow us to continue to envisage European construction along the lines that we have envisaged it up to now," he said.
Marchelli, one of nine members of the council, stressed he was speaking in a personal capacity. Only governor Jean-Claude Trichet is entitled to give the Bank's official views.

Marchelli, who wants to see the euro launched on time in 1999, said the crucial thing to watch for in Dublin would be whether EU leaders agreed on a pact to maintain budget discipline after 1999, and the nature of any agreement.
"I do not believe it can be concluded if the Germans stick to their positions," he said.
Germany has been pushing for near-automatic fines against the fiscally loose, while its partners argue there must be room for political judgment on whether a country had transgressed.
Nothing would be more terrible, Marchelli said, than to face the cold apparatus of automatic fines without the creation of a council of ministers to provide the political balance in Europe.
Otherwise the question that would arise would be whether Europe was ready to abandon democracy.
People would have to ask, "are we in the process of moving from a democracy to a technocracy?" he said.
His comments echoed those made on Monday by President Jacques Chirac who said there must be a political power to act as a counterbalance to the future European Central Bank.

While the independent central bank will set monetary policy, France has stressed that elected politicians must set exchange rate policy and wants a special council of ministers to oversee the running of economic and monetary union (EMU).

The row over the stability pact has touched a raw nerve in France, amid fears that Germany is throwing its weight around too much in favour of a currency zone run by faceless central bankers more worried about inflation than unemployment.

"French people are paying a lot of attention at the moment to what will happen in Dublin," Marchelli said. "It is up to our government...to take account of the interests of our country in this issue," he said.
"It is important that there is a strong political power as a counterbalance," he said.
Marchelli said he would like to believe there would indeed be an agreement in Dublin on the stability pact.

If not, Europe would have to await the next summit in Amsterdam in June at a time when debate was resurfacing in France on the merits of monetary union and when the European economic climate was not good.
He acknowledged that Germany's tough stance on the stability pact and other European issues had irritated some people.
"It is true that our German friends have a tendency to behave a bit like a schoolmaster. It is certain this can provoke negative reactions which could endanger European construction."
But he added, "the Germans are intelligent enough to understand this".
Marchelli also repeated that he believed the Bank of France had room to lower interest rates without waiting for a similar move from the Bundesbank.
He saw scope for a cut of as much as 50 basis points in the key intervention rate over the coming months.

"We are at 3.20, but I think that in the months to come, if we were to cut by...perhaps 20, 30 or even 50 basis points, it would not be ridiculous given current market sentiment and our (economic) fundamentals," he said.
The Bank last cut the rate, which sets the floor on money market rates, from 3.25 percent on October 31.
Marchelli is believed to be in a minority in the monetary policy council advocating faster rate cuts than those usually delivered by the ultra-cautious Bank of France.
He said he saw no need for a devaluation in the franc.
